caption: Patterns that make an audit hard

columns.label: Why a reviewer stops at it

rows.pattern: Styles that a script writes into the page
rows.example: A CSS-in-JS library in its standard setup
rows.why: The security policy must then allow inline styles, which weakens it.

rows.example: A typeface, a script or an icon set from a public CDN
rows.why: The other server learns the address of each reader. The file can also change without a review.

rows.pattern: Code that is fetched at run time
rows.example: A plugin, a template or a skill for an agent that loads from an address
rows.why: It is in no bill of materials, and no change was approved for it.

rows.pattern: Measurement and replay in the browser
rows.example: An analytics script, or a tool that records the screen of the reader
rows.why: It can take what a reader types, with no filter and no recorded reason.

rows.pattern: Code that is built from text in the browser
rows.example: A template engine that needs eval
rows.why: The security policy must then allow it, and a scanner reports that at once.

rows.pattern: A pipeline that follows moving tags
rows.example: A step named by a version tag, or a package that runs a script when it is installed
rows.why: Whoever controls the tag or the package runs code with the keys of the pipeline.

rows.example: An .env file with real keys that is shared or committed
rows.why: There is no record of who read the key, and no way to change it for one person.
